newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia recalls Iran ambassador, silent on trade.
newsitem.headline: Australia recalls Iran ambassador, silent on trade.

text.p: Australia on Friday joined other Western nations in recalling its ambassador to Iran, amid a deepening international row over a German court ruling that Tehran ordered the 1992 murders of Kurdish activists in Berlin.
Foreign Minister Alexander Downer said ambassador Stuart Hume had been ordered home immediately for consultations and briefings about the German case.

But Canberra stopped short of meeting a Labor opposition call to extend retaliation to a review of its lucrative trade with Iran, saying further response would be decided after the German court verdict was studied closely.

"Australia's response to this matter will be determined after study of the verdict and consultation with members of the European Union, as well as with other partners including the United States, Canada, Japan and New Zealand," Downer said in a statement.
"I note that the verdict in the case implicated 'the highest levels of the Iranian state' in the killings. This part of the verdict will be studied especially carefully."
Downer and Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer said Australia condemned all terrorism.
Labor opposition foreign spokesman Laurie Brereton urged the government to immediately review trade links and a A$950 million (US$750 million) line of credit to the Islamic state.
"In light of this clear evidence of state-sponsorship of international terrorism, Australia's line of credit to Iran should be terminated without delay," he said in a statement.

But two-way trade is heavily in Australia's favour -- A$650 million in Australian exports and A$28 million in imports from Iran in 1996 -- and the Australian Wheat Board warned a trade ban would hit Australia's number one wheat market, worth more than A$500 million a year.
Fischer said in a radio interview the government preferred to separate trade and politics.
"Australia does not like to trade with terrorists in any way, shape or form; what has to be made is a very careful judgment arising from a court," he said.
Downer's decision to recall Canberra's ambassador was the first outside Europe and came three weeks before German Chancellor Helmut Kohl is due to start a five-day visit.
Germany and Sweden have recalled their ambassador and the EU has invited other members to join the action.

The German court said Iran's political leadership ordered the killings of a group of Iranian Kurdish leaders in Berlin's Mykonos restaurant in 1992. It avoided names but said the assassination was ordered by a secret special operations committee whose members included Iran's president, religious leader, intelligence minister and head of foreign policy.
Germany also said it would no longer participate in a "critical dialogue" with Iran -- a European Union policy it has championed for years despite strong criticism from its allies.
Iran reacted to the verdict with similar measures -- withdrawing its ambassador and expelling four German diplomats.
